content: Shingles, also known as herpes zoster, is a condition characterized by a painful skin rash that often includes blisters. This rash typically appears on one side of the face or body and lasts for 2 to 4 weeks. The primary symptom of shingles is pain, which can be severe. Additional symptoms may include fever, headache, chills, and an upset stomach. In rare cases, shingles can lead to complications such as pneumonia, hearing problems, blindness, brain inflammation (encephalitis), or even death. Approximately 1 in 5 individuals may experience persistent severe pain after the rash resolves, a condition known as post-herpetic neuralgia. Shingles is caused by the varicella-zoster virus, the same virus responsible for chickenpox. Only individuals who have previously had chickenpox or received the chickenpox vaccine can develop shingles. After a person recovers from chickenpox, the virus remains dormant in the body and can reactivate years later, causing shingles. Shingles is not contagious in the sense that it cannot be transmitted from one person to another. However, someone who has never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine could contract chickenpox from someone with shingles, though this is uncommon. Shingles is more prevalent in individuals aged 50 and older and in those with weakened immune systems due to conditions like cancer or treatments such as steroids or chemotherapy. In the United States, at least 1 million people develop shingles each year. A vaccine for shingles was licensed in 2006. Clinical trials have shown that the vaccine prevents shingles in about half of individuals aged 60 and older. It also reduces the pain associated with shingles. A single dose of the shingles vaccine is recommended for adults aged 60 and older. Certain individuals should not receive the shingles vaccine or should delay vaccination. These include individuals who have had a life-threatening allergic reaction to gelatin, the antibiotic neomycin, or any other component of the vaccine. People with severe allergies should inform their doctor. Additionally, individuals with weakened immune systems due to conditions like HIV/AIDS, treatments such as steroids or chemotherapy, or a history of cancers affecting the bone marrow or lymphatic system (e.g., leukemia or lymphoma) should not receive the vaccine. Those with active, untreated tuberculosis or women who are pregnant or may become pregnant should also avoid the vaccine. Women should wait at least three months after receiving the vaccine before becoming pregnant. Individuals with minor illnesses, such as a cold, may still be vaccinated, but those who are moderately or severely ill should wait until they recover. As with any vaccine, the shingles vaccine may cause side effects. Serious problems, such as severe allergic reactions, are possible but extremely rare. No serious issues have been identified with the shingles vaccine to date. The vaccine is closely monitored for any unusual or severe problems. Mild side effects may include redness, soreness, swelling, or itching at the injection site (affecting about 1 in 3 people) and headache (affecting about 1 in 70 people). If a moderate or severe reaction occurs, such as a high fever or behavioral changes, medical attention should be sought immediately. Signs of a serious allergic reaction may include difficulty breathing, hoarseness or wheezing, hives, paleness, weakness, a rapid heartbeat, or dizziness. These symptoms typically occur within a few hours of vaccination. If such a reaction occurs, contact a doctor immediately and provide details about the reaction, including the date and time it occurred and when the vaccine was administered. Healthcare providers are encouraged to report adverse reactions to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS). Individuals can also report reactions directly to VAERS by calling 1-800-822-7967 or visiting their website. In rare cases where a serious reaction to a vaccine occurs, the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) provides financial assistance for medical care. For more information about the VICP, call 1-800-338-2382 or visit their website. For additional information about the shingles vaccine, consult your doctor or healthcare provider. They can provide the vaccine package insert or recommend other reliable sources. You can also contact your local or state health department’s immunization program or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) by calling 1-800-232-4636 (1-800-CDC-INFO) or visiting the National Immunization Program’s website.
